docs.title: Welcome to Rashid Jersey Store Backend
docs.text: This documentation serves as the central reference point for understanding, developing, maintaining, and extending this software system. It is intended to provide developers, contributors, and other technical stakeholders with the information necessary to work with the project confidently and consistently.

docs.title: About This Documentation
docs.text:
Software development involves more than writing code. It requires understanding architectural decisions, development workflows, technical dependencies, conventions, and the relationships between different components of a system.

This documentation aims to capture that knowledge in a structured and accessible manner. Rather than serving merely as a collection of setup instructions, it provides a record of how the project is organised, how its components interact, and how development activities should be approached.

docs.title: How to Use This Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is organised into several sections, each addressing a particular aspect of the development lifecycle.

  • Getting Started: Development environment setup, prerequisites, installation, and initial configuration.
  • Architecture: System structure, architectural decisions, application boundaries, and component relationships.
  • Development Guide: Coding conventions, implementation patterns, development workflows, and contribution guidelines.
  • Technical Reference: Frameworks, libraries, dependencies, integrations, and technical specifications.
  • Testing: Testing strategies, test organisation, execution procedures, and quality assurance.
  • Deployment and Operations: Environment management, deployment procedures, configuration, and operational considerations.
  • Project Management: Development milestones, outstanding tasks, known issues, and technical decisions.

Developers are encouraged to consult the relevant sections before introducing significant changes or extending existing functionality.

docs.title: Documentation Principles
docs.text:
This documentation is maintained as part of the project itself. It should evolve alongside the software rather than become an outdated record of how the system used to work.

The following principles guide its maintenance:

  1. Accuracy: Documented behaviour should reflect the actual implementation.
  2. Clarity: Information should be presented in a way that developers can understand and apply.
  3. Consistency: Similar components and processes should follow consistent documentation patterns.
  4. Maintainability: Documentation should be updated whenever significant implementation or architectural changes occur.
  5. Traceability: Important technical decisions should have a clear explanation of their context and rationale.

docs.title: A Note to Contributors
docs.text:
Before making changes, take time to understand the existing structure and conventions of the project. Where possible, build upon established patterns rather than introducing unnecessary alternatives.

When introducing new functionality, consider not only its immediate implementation but also its impact on existing components, maintainability, testing, and future development.

If a change introduces a new architectural decision, development convention, dependency, or significant workflow, ensure that the relevant documentation is updated.

Documentation is part of the engineering process, not an activity performed after it.

The objective is to ensure that anyone working on this project can understand not only what has been built, but also how it was built, why certain decisions were made, and how to continue developing it responsibly.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This is a backend meant to serve the functionality of a store. In the store there are three users; Administrator(ADMIN), User(USER) and Guest(GUEST). The administrator is responsible for managing the store and items within it. The user is assumed to be a regular customer who wants to frequent the store and the guest is assumed to be making one time stop at the store so the application will not store details about the Guest.

The Developer has come to the conclusion that the below activities are in scope of the behavior of the application. 1. ADMIN [] Admin should be able to manage products that others will buy.(Create, Update, Read, Delete) [] Admin should be able to manage tickets that arrive from orders placed. (Read, Update). [] Admin should recieve notifications when orders are placed [] Admin should recieve notifications when a new user registers.

  1. USER [] User should be able to place order from inventory. (Read) [] User should be able to create a cart and manage cart. (Create, Read, Update, Delete) [] User should be able to recieve notifications when they place orders. [] User should be able to recieve notifications when their orders have been delivered successfully.

  2. GUEST [] Guest should be able to place order from inventory but would go the extra mile of filling essential details needed for delivery. (read) [] Guest should be able to recieve notifications when they place orders. [] Guest should be able to recieve notifications when their orders have been delivered successfully.

  3. SYSTEM [] system should be able to create tickets when orders are placed. [] system should be able to manage inventory when orders are placed. [] system should be able to notify users, admins, guests when orders are delivered and created. [] system should be able to autofill users details on order form when they create orders. [] system should be able to log essential business actions that mutate db. [] system should be able to log errors for up to two days.

The Developer has concluded that the following are out of scope. 1. Payments. 2. Caching. 3. Shipping tracking.

Authentication - Use JWT token authentication. - use cookies.

Database - PostgreSql

Interface - React (Typescript) - Vite

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Rashid sells jerseys, sports shoes and shorts and wants a simple way for his customers to purchase from him. The best way is a web app that collates his work and allows people to purchase from him. The app should also help him organise and make delivery as an additional bonus.

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text: As the developer the solution is a django app with a react frontend. There would be two users of the system. The public facing side would be for the customers who want to purchase and the admin side for those managing the customers and products.

docs.title: SOFTWARE DESIGN AND BUILDING STRATEGY
docs.text:
The developer uses the TDD sofware development method. The idea is to ask the problem, write the test cases and then implement the solution.

I would introduce a dedicated section called Test Planning and Specifications.

docs.title: 1. Problem Definition
docs.text:
Before writing a test, establish the problem you are trying to solve.

For every feature or operation, document:

  • What problem are we addressing?
  • Under what circumstances does it occur?
  • What should the system do?
  • What should the system prevent?
  • What conditions must be satisfied?

For example, consider product creation.

Problem: Product Creation

An administrator needs to create products in the store. However, the system must ensure that incomplete or invalid product information is not persisted.

Problems to address:

  1. Products must have a valid name.
  2. Products must belong to an existing category.
  3. Duplicate product identifiers must not be accepted.
  4. Invalid data must not reach the persistence layer.
  5. Unauthorized users must not create products.

Expected outcome:

A valid product is successfully created and persisted. Invalid requests are rejected with appropriate errors.

docs.title: 2. Behaviour Specifications
docs.text:
Translate the problem into explicit expected behaviours.

I recommend using a format similar to this:

Scenario Expected behaviour Valid product data Product is created Missing product name Validation fails Invalid category Validation fails Duplicate SKU Conflict is raised Unauthorized request Access is denied

This becomes your behavioural specification.

You can also use Given-When-Then notation:

Scenario: Create a product successfully

Given an authenticated administrator
And a valid product category exists
When the administrator submits valid product data
Then the product should be created
And the product should be persisted
And the API should return HTTP 201

docs.title: 3. Test Specifications
docs.text:
Now define the actual tests you intend to write.

I would organise them according to your existing architecture.

For example:

Product Service Tests

Test Expected result test_create_product_success Product is created test_create_product_invalid_category ResourceNotFound is raised test_create_product_duplicate_sku ResourceConflict is raised test_create_product_persistence_failure Transaction is rolled back

Product API Tests

Test Expected result test_create_product_returns_201 HTTP 201 test_create_product_returns_400_for_invalid_data HTTP 400 test_create_product_requires_authentication HTTP 401 test_create_product_rejects_unauthorized_user HTTP 403

These are illustrative cases; the exact tests should reflect your actual business rules and implementation boundaries.

docs.title: 4. Test Execution and Results
docs.text:
Since you use TDD, your documentation should also track the evolution of the tests.

I would record:

  • Test identifier.
  • Test description.
  • Initial status.
  • Implementation status.
  • Final result.
  • Related feature or requirement.

For example:

Test Initial status Current status Create product successfully Failing Passing Reject invalid category Failing Passing Reject duplicate SKU Failing Passing Require authentication Failing Passing

You do not necessarily need to maintain this table manually. Your test runner and CI pipeline can provide execution results.

docs.title: 5. Testing Strategy
docs.text:
Create a separate document explaining your overall testing approach.

For your Django backend, I would consider:

Test category What it verifies Unit tests Individual functions and business logic Service tests Business operations and orchestration Repository tests Data access and persistence Serializer tests Input validation and transformation API tests HTTP contracts and permissions Integration tests Interaction between multiple components

Also document your testing tools, fixtures, test database configuration, mocking conventions and coverage expectations.

docs.title: 6. Recommended MkDocs structure
docs.text:
I would organise your testing documentation like this:

Testing/
│
├── overview.md
│
├── test-strategy.md
│
├── test-planning/
│   ├── problem-definitions.md
│   ├── behaviour-specifications.md
│   └── test-cases.md
│
├── test-implementation/
│   ├── unit-tests.md
│   ├── integration-tests.md
│   └── api-tests.md
│
└── test-execution/
    ├── running-tests.md
    └── test-results.md

docs.title: 7. One distinction I want you to appreciate
docs.text:
There are three separate things happening in your TDD workflow:

Stage 1

Problem and Behaviour Definition

What problem are we solving, and what should happen?

Stage 2

Test Design and Implementation

How will we verify that the expected behaviour is satisfied?

Stage 3

Implementation and Verification

Build the solution, run the tests, refactor, and verify that the requirements remain satisfied.

One correction worth making: in strict TDD, you write an executable test before implementing the behaviour, rather than writing a separate document containing every test and then implementing later. Your problem and behaviour specifications can be documented beforehand, while the executable tests become the authoritative verification.

My strongest recommendation: Treat your problem definitions and behavioural specifications as part of requirements engineering, and your executable tests as part of the implementation. Link them together using requirement or feature identifiers.

That gives you traceability:

Problem → Requirement → Behaviour → Test → Implementation

This is particularly valuable when you eventually revisit a feature to extend or redesign it. You can understand not only what the code does, but also what problems it was originally intended to solve and what behaviour must not regress.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The project is meant to be able to extend on Github or used when hosted.

docs.title: On Github
docs.text:
1. Locally Installing the project

    • Clone or download the repository from ikoessoun2's Jersey Store App.
    • There are two directories within the project directory; Frontend and Backend.
    • Within Frontend use npm i to install all dependencies.

    • Within Backend

      • Create a virtual environment with python -m venv .venv.
      • Activate the virtual environment with .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1.
      • Use pip install -r requirements.txt to install all dependencies in the virtual environment.

    • The frontend is meant to be built into the static/dist directory of the /backend. This is to ensure that the backend can call the frontend directly.

docs.text: For external API references use EXTERNAL API REFERENCES
